newsitem.title: PERU: Peru government, rebels hold third round of talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru government, rebels hold third round of talks.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima held a third round of talks on Saturday and agreed to meet again soon to try to end the 60-day siege.

Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, a guarantor of the talks along with Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani for the Vatican, a Red Cross envoy and an observer for Japan, told reporters: "The preliminary conversations will continue as soon as possible."

As with two previous meetings this week between Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's negotiator Domingo Palermo and the second-in-command of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), Rolly Rojas, mediators gave very few details.

In the three-hour meeting both sides finished making their proposals for the agenda of definitive talks, and the mediators "agreed to elaborate a proposal which will facilitate the continuation of the preliminary conversations," Vincent said.
Palermo and Rojas have been meeting at a Red Cross safe house opposite the besieged residence that the rebels stormed on Dec. 17, taking hostage more than 500 guests at a cocktail party.

They freed many of them but kept the most important VIPs, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers, top security officials and judges, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and about two dozen Japanese businessmen.
Mediators have been careful to term this week's talks "preliminary" but they represent a breakthrough after weeks of stalemate that followed a breakdown in dialogue on Dec. 28.

The Red Cross house has a metal detector at the door to keep guns from being taken in to the safe house, which is connected by cables with the besieged residence, apparently allowing rebel chief Nestor Cerpa Cartolini to talk by telephone to Rojas.

Despite the resumption of talks, analysts say there are no signs so far of rapprochement between two intractable positions -- the rebels' demand for 400 jailed comrades to be freed, and Fujimori's adamant refusal, encouraged by U.S. President Bill Clinton, to consider this.

In an MRTA statement sent to Reuters via electronic mail, the group claimed the crisis "is being prolonged not through the intransigence of the (rebel) command but through the intolerance of the Fujimori dictatorship and its military allies."

The communique, signed by an MRTA spokeswoman in Germany, accused Fujimori of preparing a "violent solution" and added that the government knew the MRTA would not relinquish its demand for the release of comrades in jails whose "inhuman conditions ... are a monument to infamy."

Some of the Peruvian press are interpreting Fujimori's decision to extend for another six months the work of a special committee on pardons for people wrongly jailed for terrorism as a sign that he might be ready to negotiate.
After two months' in captivity, worries about the strain on the mainly middle-aged hostages have grown. The Red Cross is treating many for hypertension, digestive problems and depression.

They have spent Christmas, New Year and now Valentine's Day away from their families. Wives and girlfriends gave the Red Cross boxes of chocolates for the men on Friday and 72 couples were married at a mass wedding to show solidarity with them.
The Red Cross gave details on Saturday of its mammoth aid operation to the hostages inside the residence.
The organisation said that so far it has enabled the captives to send 2,238 messages to their families, while relatives had sent 2,583 missives into the compound.

It also has delivered 1,201 packages of clothing, 12,914 meals -- including 4,651 Japanese dishes -- 3,454 litres (912 gallons) of hot water for making tea and coffee, 16,180 litres (4,274 gallons) of drinking water, and 509 copies of various sports' newspapers.
The food aid included 299 loaves of bread, 4,230 portions of cheese, 1,380 oranges, 3,390 bananas and 2,840 apples.
